tagline.text: A grand rock sculpture garden shaped by Pacific waves over ages

children.text: An island in the San Bernardino Strait off Northern Samar, famous for seven massive rock formations carved by Pacific waves and wind, and its clear tide pools. With few tourists so far, it remains a hidden gem of Eastern Visayas where you can encounter untouched nature.

Biri Island lies in the San Bernardino Strait, at the northern tip of Samar Island, between Luzon's Sorsogon and Samar. Administratively part of the municipality of Biri in Northern Samar, the main island and its surrounding small islands together make up a single municipality. The island's north coast takes the full force of waves rolling in from the Pacific, and over long ages the rock there has been carved and hollowed out, creating sculpture-like rock formations found almost nowhere else in the Philippines.

These rock formations are collectively called the "Biri Rock Formations," and from west to east the seven are Magasang, Maqueda, Macadlaw, Puhunan, Bel-at, Caranas, and Pinanahawan. Some rise like walls tens of meters high, others have been punched through by waves to make huge windows, and emerald tide pools collect between the rocks. The island was designated the Biri-Larosa Protected Landscape and Seascape in
and is managed as such.

Biri's rock formations can only be properly explored at low tide. When the water recedes, sand flats and rock shelves beneath the formations are exposed for walking; at high tide, waves crash against the rocks, shooting spray high into the air. The dramatic way the scenery changes with the tide and waves is this place's charm.

With poor transport links and few amenities, group tourists are still rare here. That makes it a strong recommendation for travelers wanting to see the Philippines' raw natural side, photographers after distinctive rock formations, and those wanting to experience the quiet island-village life of Samar. Basic fitness and sturdy shoes are needed for climbing over the rocks.

blocks.title: Bel-at rock and its tide pool

children.text: Biri's most famous spot, where a clear tide pool appears beneath a massive rock at low tide, perfect for swimming. Beyond the pool, the sight of waves crashing into the rock and shooting up spray is overwhelming.

One of the tallest and most majestic formations; following a guide up through the rock crevices reveals a sweeping view of the Pacific and the strait. The climb is steep and sharp, so gloves and grippy shoes are needed.

blocks.title: The split rock crevice of Magsapad

children.text: Waves have carved deep crevices and cave-like spaces into the rock here, making for fun exploration. The blue sea glimpsed through the gaps is a favorite photo spot.
Waves have bored openings and arches here, popular for photos framing the sea through the gap. It's inaccessible at high tide, so time your visit to low tide.
The path to the rock formations crosses a wooden boardwalk over a mangrove forest. You can observe the mangrove ecosystem's crabs, mudskippers, and small fish along the way.

blocks.title: Walking the rock shelves at low tide

children.text: At the lowest point of the tide, wide rock shelves and sand flats between the formations are exposed and connect on foot. You can see intertidal creatures like sea urchins, sea cucumbers, and starfish.

children.text: Spend the evening at the beach in Biri's town proper, and ask your homestay to cook fish and crab freshly caught by local fishermen for dinner.

From Manila it is more usual to go via Cebu than direct, and some routes, like the one from Clark, are on and off, so check before booking. one way. Departure times are fixed and there may be no late-afternoon boats, so it's safer to reach the port during the morning. If your group is large or the schedule doesn't match, you can charter a bangka, often quoted around

From Biri port to the north coast where the rock formations are, travel is by habal-habal (motorcycle taxi). For 3 people, a round trip costs about
, negotiated on the condition the driver waits with your guide. Between the formations, you move on foot along the mangrove boardwalk and rock shelves.
Biri Island sits where the Pacific meets the strait, so sea conditions dictate the trip. From
March
to
June
, waves are comparatively calm and rain is light, making bangka trips and rock exploration most reliable. Tide pool water is at its clearest on sunny days in this period.
From
October
to
February

, the strong northeast monsoon (Amihan) whips up very high waves on the Pacific side and brings frequent rain. This is when you can see the spectacular sight of waves crashing into the rocks, but bangka cancellations and restricted rock access are common. From
July
to
November
is typhoon season, so always check the forecast. Whatever the season, the key is checking a tide table and planning around days and times with low, receding tides.

Biri Island itself has almost no hotels; there are a few small homestays and guesthouses around city hall and the coast, at about

per night, mostly fan rooms with no hot water or air conditioning to speak of. Asking at the tourism office can get you referred to a registered homestay. For more comfortable lodging, you can stay in Allen or Catarman (about
per night) and visit as a day trip, though matching the low tide can be difficult due to boat schedules — staying overnight on the island is recommended instead.

With few restaurants on the island, most meals are handled at your homestay. Buying fish, crab, or squid at the port in the morning and asking your homestay host to cook it lets you eat fresh seafood cheaply. Samar's coconut-milk dishes (ginataan) and kinilaw (raw fish ceviche) are local staples. It's best to buy snacks and bottled water in advance at Lavezares or Allen.
Check a tide table beforehand and plan to arrive at the rock formations within
2–3 hours
of the lowest tide.
Biri Island has no ATMs, so withdraw enough cash in Catarman or Allen beforehand.
The rocks are sharp and slippery, so bring aqua shoes or thick-soled trekking sandals and thin gloves.
There's almost no shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen, and at least 2 liters of water.
Cell signal is weak in some areas, so confirm boat times and your guide's contact in advance.
A wide-angle lens or your phone's wide mode helps capture the massive scale of the rocks, and including a person in the shot gives a sense of size.
Put electronics in a waterproof bag, since spray is heavy during the bangka ride and around the rocks.
The Biri tourism office's Facebook page frequently posts updates on boat schedules and rule changes, so check before departing.
To the Waray people, the rocks of Biri are a sacred place where the goddess Verbinota lives. If a guide asks you not to make loud noises in front of the rocks, it is courteous to comply.
Never stand at the edge of a rock where the tide is rising or big waves are crashing in. Pacific-side waves can surge without warning and have swept people off the rocks.
A registered local guide is mandatory when visiting the rock formations, and you must not enter areas your guide marks off-limits.
Only swim in the tide pools when your guide judges it safe at low tide, and get out immediately if waves start washing over.
As a protected landscape, scratching or writing on the rocks, collecting coral or shells, and littering are prohibited.
The island has no proper hospital, so injuries require traveling to the main island. Bring basic first-aid and disinfectant supplies.
Bangkas are canceled by coast guard order in bad weather, so it's safer to be off the island the day before your return flight.
